H1.text: A ball tossed to a friend. Water from a hose. A long jumper in the air.

H2.text: All three curve in the very same way. Why that shape?

H3.text: Aarav tests it on his study table. He flicks one coin off the edge, and lets another coin fall at the same moment.

H4.text: The flicked coin flies far. The other drops straight down. Which one hits the floor first?

H5.text: Most people say the dropped coin. Let's find out, and see exactly why.

P2.text: It is any object that is thrown, and then moves only under gravity.

P3.text: A thrown ball, a long jumper, a catapult stone. Once released, only gravity pulls on them.

P4.text: A rocket with its engine on is not a projectile. The engine still pushes. We also ignore air resistance.

S1.text: Aarav's test on the motion notebook. Two balls, same height, same moment.

S2.text: The dark ball is just dropped. The blue ball is pushed sideways at five metres per second.

S3.text: Watch the heights. At every flash, both balls are at the same level.

S4.text: They land together, after one second. The height graph for both is the same curve.

S5.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze, and draw the velocities.

S6.text: Sideways, the blue arrow never changes. Five metres per second, all the way.

S7.text: Downwards, the violet arrow grows by nine point eight metres per second, every second. Exactly like the dropped ball.

S8.text: Your turn. Push the blue ball three times faster. Does it land sooner, later, or at the same time? Pause and decide.

S9.text: The same time! A faster push sends it farther, not faster down. Fall time depends only on height.

A1.text: Now let's throw at an angle, like a real throw.

A2.text: Speed twenty metres per second, at thirty degrees above the ground.

A3.text: Split the throw into two parts. Across, u cos theta. Up, u sin theta.

A4.text: Across, that is about seventeen point three metres per second. Up, it is ten.

A5.text: Let it fly. The across speed stays the same. The up speed shrinks to zero at the top, then grows downwards.

A6.text: And gravity, the red arrow, points down the whole time. At the start, at the top, and at the end.

D1.text: Now the rules, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Split the start velocity. u x equals u cos theta. u y equals u sin theta.

D3.text: Step two. Across, there is no acceleration. So x equals u cos theta, times t.

D4.text: Step three. Up and down, the acceleration is g, downwards. So y equals u sin theta t, minus half g t squared.

D5.text: Step four. The velocity parts. v x stays u cos theta. And v y equals u sin theta minus g t.

T1.text: Remember this. One throw, two motions. Steady across, free fall up and down.

K1.text: Side by side. Across, the ball moves like a car on cruise control. Same gap every tick.

K2.text: Up and down, it moves like a ball thrown straight up. It slows, stops, and falls back.

K3.text: Now you try. At the very top of the path, is the speed of the ball zero? Pause and decide.

K4.text: No! Only the up and down part is zero. The across part, u cos theta, remains. So the top speed is u cos theta.

W2.text: A ball is thrown at twenty metres per second, at thirty degrees. Find its position and velocity at one point five seconds.

W3.text: Across. x equals seventeen point three times one point five. About twenty six metres.

W4.text: Up. y equals ten times one point five, minus half g times one point five squared. About four metres.

W5.text: Velocity. v x stays seventeen point three. v y is ten minus nine point eight times one point five, minus four point seven. So it is coming down.

W6.text: Speed is the root of seventeen point three squared plus four point seven squared. About eighteen metres per second.

X2.text: Many students say that at the highest point, the acceleration is zero, because the ball stops going up.

X3.text: But gravity never switches off. The acceleration is g, downwards, at every point, even at the top.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In questions on a projectile's position or velocity at a given time, and its direction.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A ball is thrown at thirty metres per second, at fifty three degrees. Sine fifty three is point eight, and g is ten. When is its velocity perpendicular to its starting velocity? Pause and solve.

B1.text: The answer is B. Three point seven five seconds.

B2.text: Split the start velocity. Across, eighteen. Up, twenty four.

B3.text: Perpendicular means the dot product is zero. Eighteen times eighteen, plus twenty four times, twenty four minus ten t, is zero.

B4.text: So two forty t is nine hundred, and t is three point seven five seconds. The flight lasts four point eight, so it is still flying.

Y3.text: Two. What is the speed of a projectile at its highest point?
